title: How I Do All My Dev Work With Grok Bot
description:
Wanted to show how I'm orchestrating projects/agents through Grok Bot. It's kinda become my primary interface for T3 Code (Codex/Claude Code) and everything else.

Thank you Firecrawl for sponsoring! Check them out at: https://davis7.link/firecrawl

grok bot prompt example - https://x.com/davis7/status/2117069521144172599

My X, Discord, and more: https://davis7.sh/
summary:
Workflow and real example | 00:00–06:31: Ben Davis uses Grok Bot as a persistent cloud-based chat interface to delegate coding to Cursor cloud agents or T3 Code on his own machines. For an unreleased group-chat project he requested five homepage drafts and separately launched two sidebar threads; the agents opened pull requests and returned links. A preview artifact initially contained blurry images and none of the designs was quite right, so human feedback was still necessary. The Firecrawl segment is sponsored, not an independent comparison.

Architecture and setup | 06:32–10:17: He moved away from a few overloaded general-purpose bots to one bot per real project, each holding its repository, routines and context. Cursor cloud agents communicate natively with Grok Bot; he often prefers T3 Code because it reuses his own environment and Claude Code/Codex subscriptions. His demonstrated connection uses a T3 Connect MCP URL and cloud sign-in, with LAN and Tailscale preferred ahead of the cloud connection afterward; he cautions that setup may change.

Verification infrastructure | 10:18–14:58: His project uses Alchemy to simulate infrastructure locally and create per-PR Cloudflare preview environments, with CI tearing resources down when a PR closes or merges. He describes centralizing secrets with Infisical and keeping a separate no-environment-variable local development path so agents can run the application and take screenshots. He favors interactive and end-to-end checks over many unit tests; that is his preference, not evidence that unit tests are unnecessary.

Review loop and verdict | 14:59–18:04: His agents record the harness, model and orchestrator in PRs, while CI and review bots provide additional checks before he tries the actual preview. He spots a low-reasoning setting he did not intend and, despite describing a wait-for-all-checks policy, merges the example without waiting for one review bot. Davis says the setup requires substantial upfront project work but has greatly improved his own productivity, letting him request changes from his phone; he reports no measured productivity benchmark.
why_valuable: Helps decide whether to adopt a phone-accessible agent-orchestration workflow, and which project-specific preview, secret-management and review safeguards to build before trusting its pull requests.
key_takeaways: 00:49–01:01: Grok Bot is the orchestrator, not the coding environment; Davis connects it to Cursor cloud agents and T3 Code on his machines.
01:49–06:15: Five homepage drafts and two sidebar threads show parallel delegation, but blurry preview images and imperfect designs still required human feedback.
06:32–08:00: A dedicated bot per project avoids the clutter Davis encountered with a few all-purpose bots and keeps repository context together.
08:28–09:35: He favors T3 Code for reuse of existing Claude Code/Codex subscriptions and his own environment; his demonstrated MCP connection uses T3 Connect authentication.
10:18–12:36: Per-PR staging previews and automatic resource teardown make it easier to inspect agent changes without relying solely on a code diff.

13:03–14:39: Central secrets and a no-secret local simulation help agents run and visually test the app; Davis prefers behavioral checks, though this does not establish that unit tests can safely be omitted.
14:59–16:49: Record agent configuration, run CI and review bots, and test the live preview; Davis nonetheless merged his example before one bot finished.
16:52–17:45: He reports a productivity improvement but emphasizes substantial upfront setup and provides no measured benchmark.

chapters.title: A phone-first development control room
chapters.description: Davis describes a cloud bot that coordinates his personal, business and development work through chat, connecting to Cursor and T3 Code. He gives an unreleased group-chat app as an example and requests five different homepage drafts, illustrating how a phone can initiate substantial development work.

chapters.title: Sponsored web research with Firecrawl
chapters.description: In a paid sponsorship, Davis says his agents use Firecrawl to search, crawl sites and turn pages into cleaner Markdown rather than consuming raw JavaScript and CSS. He also promotes its tools and Alexandria data sources; these are sponsor claims rather than independently demonstrated comparisons.

chapters.title: Parallel pull requests and imperfect previews
chapters.description: A Cursor agent handles homepage drafts while two T3 Code threads tackle sidebar changes, with resulting pull requests routed back through the bot. The HTML preview artifact has blurry images and the designs are not yet what Davis wants, so he requests fixes and reviews the live alternatives himself.

chapters.title: Project-specific bots and coding connections
chapters.description: A small set of general-purpose bots became cluttered, so Davis now gives each substantial project its own bot, repository link and working context. Cursor agents can exchange messages with it directly, while T3 Code lets him reuse his own machines and coding subscriptions for delegated work.

chapters.title: Connecting a local machine via MCP
chapters.description: Davis demonstrates selecting T3 Connect in the environment settings, copying the machine's MCP URL to the bot and completing cloud authentication. He then restores LAN and Tailscale ahead of T3 Connect in the connection order, and notes that the setup process could change.

chapters.title: Build disposable staging environments
chapters.description: Because he does not closely read every large agent-generated change, Davis wants a working preview attached to each pull request. He describes Alchemy-based local infrastructure simulation and Cloudflare preview deployments created by CI and torn down when the PR closes or merges, allowing actual behavior to be checked.

chapters.title: Secrets and runnable local simulations
chapters.description: Davis centralizes environment variables in Infisical, with separate development, staging and production environments, rather than distributing large environment files. His project also runs locally without environment variables, enabling agents to launch the application and inspect it; his preference for behavioral testing over many unit tests is a judgment, not a general proof.

chapters.title: Human review, automated checks and final verdict
chapters.description: A sidebar pull request records its harness and model, but Davis spots an unintended low-reasoning setting before testing the theme toggle in its preview. He describes CI, end-to-end tests and review bots as confidence checks, yet merges without waiting for one review; he concludes the upfront setup has made his own phone-based workflow much more productive without presenting a measured benchmark.
